title: The Transaction Lifecycle, Trust Funds & Career Launch
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.
note: Includes integrated capstone items drawing on multiple units.

questions.stem: Trust funds received by a broker must be placed into escrow, a trust account, or the hands of the principal not later than:
options: The end of the business day received
rationales: Same-day deposit is best practice but is not the regulatory deadline.
Correct. The three-business-day rule governs deposits of trust funds by a broker or the broker's salesperson.
Five days exceeds the regulatory window.
Ten days exceeds the regulatory window.

questions.stem: A buyer's $25,000 deposit reaches the brokerage Friday at 4 p.m. with written instructions to hold the check uncashed until acceptance. The seller accepts Monday. The deposit deadline runs from:
options: Friday, when the check was received
Monday, when the offer was accepted
The date the buyer's contingencies are removed
rationales: A properly disclosed instruction to hold the check pending acceptance postpones the obligation past receipt.
Correct. When the offer directs the check be held uncashed and the seller is informed of that instruction, the three-business-day clock runs from acceptance.
The regulatory deadline is not tied to escrow's opening.
Contingency removal occurs well after the deposit obligation attaches.

questions.stem: A broker deposits a client's earnest money into the brokerage's general operating account over a weekend, then transfers it to the trust account Monday with no loss to anyone. The broker has committed:
options: No violation, because the funds were restored
rationales: Restoration does not cure the violation; the mixing itself is the offense.
Correct. Placing trust funds in the broker's own account is commingling, disciplinable even when no client suffers a loss and the funds are promptly restored.
Conversion requires actually using the funds for another purpose, which did not occur here.
No allowance permits routing trust funds through a general business account.

questions.stem: A broker uses a client's trust funds to cover the brokerage payroll, intending to replace the money next month. This is:
options: Conversion, supporting revocation and criminal charges
rationales: Commingling is mixing; here the funds were actually spent, which is the more serious offense.
Correct. Using trust funds for another purpose is conversion, grounds for license revocation and criminal prosecution.
Trust funds may never be borrowed by the broker.
Repayment with interest does not cure misappropriation.

questions.stem: A broker's monthly trust account reconciliation must show agreement among:
options: The bank statement and the broker's tax return
The control record, the sum of all beneficiary ledgers, and the bank statement
The listing agreements and the escrow instructions
The commission ledger and the operating account
rationales: Tax filings are unrelated to trust fund reconciliation.
Correct. All three must agree, and the reconciliation must be performed monthly in writing and retained — a leading DRE audit finding when it is missing.
Contracts are transaction records, not trust accounting records.
The operating account is separate from trust funds by definition.

questions.stem: A trust account holds funds for eight beneficiaries. The broker disburses more than one beneficiary's balance, causing that ledger to go negative while total account funds remain positive. This is:
options: Acceptable, because the account overall is positive
Conversion, because one beneficiary's funds were used for another
A bookkeeping error with no regulatory consequence
rationales: A positive overall balance does not excuse a negative individual ledger.
Correct. Using one beneficiary's funds to cover another's disbursement is conversion; no beneficiary's balance may ever go negative.
The violation goes beyond mixing — client funds were actually applied to another's obligation.
Negative beneficiary balances are a serious violation, not a harmless error.

questions.stem: Brokerage transaction records must generally be retained for:
rationales: One year is insufficient under the Real Estate Law.
Correct. Brokers must retain transaction records for three years, running from closing or from the listing date where no closing occurred.
Seven years is a common tax retention period, not the brokerage requirement.
Indefinite retention is prudent for some records but is not the regulatory standard.

questions.stem: On a settlement statement, the purchase price appears as a:
options: Debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
Credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller
rationales: Correct. The buyer owes the price (debit) and the seller receives it (credit).
This reverses the entries.
The price cannot be an obligation of both parties.
The price cannot be a benefit to both parties.

questions.stem: At closing on a rental property, tenant security deposits held by the seller are:
options: Prorated as of the closing date
Transferred in full as a debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
Paid directly to the tenants at closing
rationales: Security deposits are never prorated; they are the tenants' money in full.
Correct. Deposits transfer in their entirety, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer, who assumes the obligation to account to the tenants.
The seller cannot keep funds belonging to tenants.
Deposits are not refunded at sale; the obligation passes to the new owner.

questions.stem: A sale closes June 20 with the buyer owning the day of closing. The seller prepaid $9,180 in annual taxes for the fiscal year beginning July 1. Using a 360-day year, the proration is:
rationales: Correct. Daily = 9,180 ÷ 360 = 25.50. Seller owned July 1 through June 19 = 349 days = $8,899.50 consumed; the prepaid remainder of $280.50 benefits the buyer and is credited to the seller.
$8,899.50 is the seller's own consumed share, not the amount reimbursed.
The direction is reversed — a prepaid expense produces a seller credit.
$4,590 is half the annual bill and corresponds to no step here.

questions.stem: Unpaid property taxes that accrued during the seller's ownership appear at closing as a:
options: Credit to the seller and debit to the buyer
Debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
rationales: Prepaid taxes produce a seller credit; these taxes are unpaid.
Correct. An accrued but unpaid expense is charged to the seller and credited to the buyer, who will pay the bill when it comes due.
Only one party bears the accrued obligation.
Taxes are the most commonly prorated closing item.

questions.stem: In a California transaction, title passes to the buyer upon:
rationales: The purchase agreement creates contract rights, not title.
Loan signing is a step toward funding, not the transfer of title.
Correct. Close of escrow occurs at recording, which is when title passes and after which escrow disburses.
Possession may be delivered before or after closing and does not determine title.

questions.stem: A trustee of a family trust sells a home she personally occupied for six years and knows the roof leaks. The sale is TDS-exempt as a fiduciary transfer. She must:
options: Say nothing, since the exemption applies
Disclose the known leak, because the form exemption does not excuse concealing known material facts
Disclose only if the buyer requests a TDS
Disclose only to the buyer's agent
rationales: A form exemption is never a knowledge exemption.
Correct. A transferor with actual knowledge of a material defect must disclose it regardless of any exemption from the statutory form.
The duty is affirmative and does not depend on a buyer's request.
Disclosure must reach the buyer, not merely the buyer's agent informally.

questions.stem: A seller wants to negotiate with two buyers at once without risk of forming two binding contracts. She should use:
options: A multiple counteroffer form requiring her final acceptance
A backup offer addendum with each
rationales: Sending ordinary counteroffers to two buyers risks binding her twice if both accept.
Correct. A multiple counteroffer provides that no contract forms until the seller signs a final acceptance of one buyer's response, preserving her choice.
Backup offers address what happens after a primary contract fails.
Options require consideration and would bind her to sell.

questions.stem: A salesperson closes a transaction. Escrow should disburse the commission to:
options: The salesperson and broker in their agreed shares
rationales: A salesperson may not be paid directly for licensed activity by escrow.
Correct. Escrow pays the brokerages; the broker then compensates the salesperson under their written agreement — a salesperson may accept compensation only from their employing broker.
Escrow does not split commissions inside a brokerage.
The salesperson has no authority to redirect commission payments.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST practice for a broker holding a small amount of personal funds in the trust account?
options: Keep several months of operating capital there for convenience
Keep only a limited amount to cover bank service charges, as regulations permit
Keep personal funds equal to the largest client balance
rationales: Holding operating capital in the trust account is commingling.
Correct. Regulations permit only a limited amount of the broker's own funds to cover bank service charges; that narrow allowance is the sole intentional mixing permitted.
Leaving earned commissions in the trust account beyond a limited period is commingling.
No provision ties permitted personal funds to client balances.

questions.stem: During a DRE audit, the MOST common trust fund findings involve:
options: Missing monthly reconciliations, absent per-beneficiary ledgers, and late deposits
rationales: Outright theft is rare compared with recordkeeping failures.
Correct. Audit findings are typically mundane: reconciliations not performed, ledgers not maintained per beneficiary, deposits made late, and personal funds left in the account.
E&O coverage is a business and brokerage matter, not a trust fund audit finding.
Advertising issues arise under separate rules, not trust fund audits.

questions.stem: For a newly licensed salesperson choosing a first brokerage, the factor that generally matters MOST is:
options: Training, mentorship, and the quality of broker supervision
The size of the national brand
rationales: A high split with no support is worth less than a lower split with real guidance, especially before the first closings.
Correct. For a new licensee, training and accessible supervision outweigh split, because the responsible broker's oversight both develops competence and protects against liability.
Brand recognition does not substitute for supervision and training.
Low fees do not help an agent who has no transactions and no one to consult.

questions.stem: A capstone transaction closes at $845,000 with no assumed loan. At $0.55 per $500, the county documentary transfer tax is:
rationales: $464.75 applies $0.55 per $1,000 rather than per $500.
Correct. 845,000 ÷ 500 = 1,690 increments; 1,690 × $0.55 = $929.50. With no assumed loan, the full price is taxed.
$1,859.00 doubles the correct figure, which would reflect an added city tax at the same rate.
$4,225.00 is 0.5% of the price and corresponds to no standard rate.

questions.stem: A seller instructs her agent to prefer 'a nice family, not investors.' The agent should understand that:
options: Both preferences are lawful because the seller owns the property
Preferring owner-occupants over investors is lawful, but preferring a 'family' implicates familial status and cannot be honored
Either preference is lawful if documented in the file
rationales: Ownership creates no exemption from fair housing law for a protected characteristic.
Correct. Investor status is not a protected characteristic, so an owner-occupant preference is lawful; familial status is protected, so the 'family' preference must be refused.
The investor preference is lawful; only the familial status preference is not.
Documenting an unlawful instruction does not authorize following it.
